scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Shake emerged in the mid-1960s as a prominent fad dance closely associated with the British Mod subculture.
Evolving out of the blue beat style, the dance surged in popularity across youth venues and nightspots, officially superseding the Twist by 1965.
Unlike earlier partner dances, The Shake reflected a cultural shift toward heightened individualism on the dance floor.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The Shake served as a social release mechanism for 1960s youth, exemplifying individualistic expression without the constraints of formal partner dancing.

The hypnotic combination of loud music and intense somatic vibration offered a immersive experience that intrigued contemporary researchers studying the effects of music on the human central nervous system.
Today it is a historical tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Characterized by a signature 'tense jerkiness,' The Shake involved virtually no structured steps or codified choreography.
Dancers stood individually without a partner, maintaining an erratic, trembling posture through the legs while letting the head shake freely.
Arms gesticulated arbitrarily to the rhythm, leaving full creative freedom to the individual dancer.
Watch for Head Shake, Leg Tremble.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While individual dancers were non-professional participants in the Mod scene, musician and composer Laurie Johnson stands out for capturing the movement's sonic marker in his 1965 album 'The Shake LP'.
Sociologist Frances Rust documented the dance's physiological and social impact in contemporary research.
The Shake evolved directly from the blue beat style within the Mod scene and displaced the Twist as the dominant British fad dance of 1965.
